title: Delhi High Court Stops FSSAI Action Against Emami's 'Healthy & Tasty' Edible Oil Claims
meta_description: Justice Amit Mahajan restrains FSSAI from acting against Emami Agrotech over its 'Healthy & Tasty' edible oil branding, questioning the notice's reasoning.
case_name: Emami Agrotech Limited v. Union of India & Ors.
body: Edible oil buyers in India see the brand name Healthy & Tasty on bottles of sunflower oil and kachchi ghani, or cold-pressed, mustard oil sold by Emami Agrotech. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India decided the name itself was a problem worth chasing. It issued a show cause notice on 5 June 2026 asking Emami to explain why using that label on its packaging did not mislead a buyer about what the oil could do for them, treating the words as an implied health and nutritional claim that the company had not backed up under the governing labelling regulations.

A show cause notice ordinarily gives a company a chance to answer before anything happens on the ground, and Emami took that chance seriously. It sent its reply on 23 June 2026, setting out why the brand name, in its view, was ordinary marketing language rather than a regulated health claim requiring separate scientific substantiation. FSSAI did not rule on that reply one way or the other. Instead, on 17 July 2026, it wrote directly to the state food safety commissioners and asked them to proceed with enforcement action against products carrying the Healthy & Tasty mark, skipping over the explanation Emami had already filed weeks earlier.

That sequence, more than the original notice, is what pushed the company into the Delhi High Court. Emami's writ petition attacked both documents together, the June show cause notice and the July enforcement letter, arguing that a regulator cannot ask its field officers to act against a product while the company's answer to the very notice justifying that action still sits undecided on file. Counsel for Emami told the court that enforcement at this stage, before the regulator had even disposed of the reply, would cause irreversible commercial harm to an established edible oil brand over a labelling question that had not been finally adjudicated by anyone.

Justice Mahajan did not have to go far to find the notice short on reasoning. On a prima facie reading, the show cause notice did not spell out how the particular combination of words amounted to a misleading health claim, as distinct from a generic marketing phrase of the kind many packaged food brands carry on their labels without objection. The order does not hold that the branding is compliant with the Food Safety and Standards Act or the labelling regulations framed under it. It holds only that FSSAI has not yet shown, even on the face of its own notice, how the branding falls foul of them.

On that limited but telling finding, the court restrained FSSAI from taking any coercive or precipitate step against Emami over the Healthy & Tasty branding until the writ petition comes up again, with the matter listed for hearing in February 2027. Emami continues selling its oils under the existing label in the meantime, and the state commissioners who received the July letter cannot act on it against this company while the restraint stands. The underlying question, whether the brand name is itself an unsubstantiated claim, remains open and will be argued out at the next hearing rather than decided now.

Emami was fighting a near-identical battle in Calcutta at almost the same time, over the same underlying notice. On 6 October 2026, the Calcutta High Court gave Emami Agrotech protection from coercive action in connection with that FSSAI notice, listing its own proceeding for 25 November 2026. Two High Courts, within days of each other, each found enough in Emami's case to pause FSSAI's hand on the ground, though neither has cleared the branding on its merits or guaranteed that Emami will succeed when the matters are argued out in full.

This dispute sits inside a wider push by FSSAI against packaged food labelling across the industry this year. ITC secured comparable relief over the '100 per cent' claim on its Aashirvaad atta, and Dabur obtained a stay on a prohibitory order touching its own '100 per cent' marketing language, both before the labelling questions in those matters were finally decided. Read together with the Emami orders, these cases are not a verdict on any one brand's honesty. They tell FSSAI that a show cause notice has to carry its own reasoning before a court will let an enforcement letter follow it, and they give packaged food companies a tested route to interim protection while that reasoning is tested in court.
why_it_matters: Food businesses often treat a show cause notice from FSSAI as a near-final step before enforcement, since the regulator can direct state commissioners to act on it. This order confirms that a notice still has to show its own reasoning, specifically how a brand name or claim misleads a consumer, before courts will let enforcement follow. Packaged food companies facing labelling notices now have a tested route to interim protection while that reasoning is tested, provided they move before state officers act on a follow-up enforcement letter.
card_summary: Delhi High Court restrains FSSAI from acting against Emami Agrotech's 'Healthy & Tasty' edible oil branding, finding the regulator's notice did not explain how the name misleads buyers.
card_tip: A food safety show cause notice must explain how a label or claim is misleading before enforcement can follow; challenge an enforcement letter issued without deciding your reply.
verification_notes: Bar & Bench, LiveLaw Biz, LawChakra and LawBeat agree on: the 15 October 2026 date of Justice Amit Mahajan's order, the products involved (sunflower oil and kachchi ghani mustard oil under Healthy & Tasty), the 5 June 2026 show cause notice, the 17 July 2026 letter to state food safety commissioners, the restraint on coercive action, and the prima facie finding that the notice did not explain how the mark was misleading. The W.P.(C) 15491/2026 case number is given by only one of the four sources reviewed (LiveLaw-sourced reporting); it is reported here as such and flagged rather than treated as fully cross-verified. The next listing date is given as February 2027 by the sources that specify a year; one source says only 'February' without a year, which is consistent rather than conflicting. The parallel Calcutta High Court order of 6 October 2026 and its 25 November 2026 listing, and the ITC and Dabur '100 per cent' claim matters, are reported consistently across the same set of sources and are included as background context, not as holdings of this order.
